MEAL PERIOD WAIVER — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

MEAL PERIOD WAIVER DECLARATION
Jordan Lee and Acme, Inc. state as follows regarding Jordan Lee's meal period for a workday with a total scheduled work period of 5 hours. Jordan Lee and Acme, Inc. mutually and voluntarily agree to waive the meal period otherwise required for that workday, as and to the extent permitted by California law for a work period of this length. This waiver reflects the genuine, voluntary agreement of both Jordan Lee and Acme, Inc.; it is not made a condition of Jordan Lee's continued employment, and neither party has been pressured, threatened, or offered an incentive to enter into it.

THE STATUTORY WAIVER THRESHOLDS
Cal. Labor Code § 512(a) permits a meal period to be waived in exactly two circumstances, both tied to shift length. First, if Jordan Lee's total work period for the day is no more than six hours, the otherwise-required first meal period may be waived by mutual consent of Acme, Inc. and Jordan Lee. Second, if Jordan Lee works more than 10 hours but no more than 12 hours in a day, the second meal period (otherwise required for a shift over 10 hours) may be waived by mutual consent of Acme, Inc. and Jordan Lee — but only if the first meal period was not itself waived. There is no statutory waiver available for a shift longer than 12 hours, and the second-meal-period waiver is unavailable on any shift, however short, if the first meal period was waived.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "An employer shall not employ an employee for a work period of more than five hours per day without providing the employee with a meal period of not less than 30 minutes, except that if the total work period per day of the employee is no more than six hours, the meal period may be waived by mutual consent of both the employer and employee. An employer shall not employ an employee for a work period of more than 10 hours per day without providing the employee with a second meal period of not less than 30 minutes, except that if the total hours worked is no more than 12 hours, the second meal period may be waived by mutual consent of the employer and the employee only if the first meal period was not waived."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 512(a), Cal. Lab. Code § 512, subd. (a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=512.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Labor Code § 512(a)), offered as documented evidence of what that provision says — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee. Federal law imposes no meal-period requirement at all, and most other states either have no meal-break statute or a far less detailed one. This clause quotes the same statutory subsection already quoted in full in this corpus's separate Meal and Rest Break Policy document (its meal_period_requirement clause); it is restated here, standing alone, because this information sheet is meant to be usable independently, not because it is offered as a second, independent source for the same text. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 512(a)); no additional independent source was found for this specific text.

"MUTUAL CONSENT" — WHETHER A WRITING IS REQUIRED
The statutory text of Cal. Labor Code § 512(a) conditions both meal-period waivers described above on "mutual consent of both the employer and employee" — it does not, in these words, require that consent be documented in writing. By contrast, elsewhere in the same body of law, where a writing is required for a different kind of meal-period arrangement, the text says so explicitly: a wage-order provision governing health care industry employees who work shifts of more than eight hours conditions a related but separate meal-period waiver on the waiver being "documented in a written agreement that is voluntarily signed by both the employee and the employer." The bare § 512(a) waiver described above is not made subject to that same written-and-signed language.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "An employer shall not employ an employee for a work period of more than five hours per day without providing the employee with a meal period of not less than 30 minutes, except that if the total work period per day of the employee is no more than six hours, the meal period may be waived by mutual consent of both the employer and employee."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 512(a), Cal. Lab. Code § 512, subd. (a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=512.)
  "Notwithstanding any other provision of this order, employees in the health care industry who work shifts in excess of eight (8) total hours in a workday may voluntarily waive their right to one of their two meal periods. In order to be valid, any such waiver must be documented in a written agreement that is voluntarily signed by both the employee and the employer."
  — IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 11(D), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 11(D) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle04.pdf)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute and one state's regulation (Cal. Labor Code § 512(a) and IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001 § 11(D)), offered as documented evidence of what those provisions say — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee, and not a claim that no court has ever read an unstated writing requirement into § 512(a)'s bare text. These two citations are genuinely independent instruments (a Labor Code statute and a separate Industrial Welfare Commission wage order provision), not subsections of the same source. Separately, and without a citable source for it, many employers document meal-period waivers in writing as a matter of practice or evidentiary caution — that is a risk-management choice, not itself a statutory command, and is not asserted here as one.

ON-DUTY MEAL PERIODS ARE A DIFFERENT ARRANGEMENT THAN A WAIVER
An "on-duty" meal period is analytically distinct from waiving a meal period under Cal. Labor Code § 512(a). Waiving a meal period means the meal period does not happen at all and is not paid separately. An on-duty meal period, by contrast, means Jordan Lee remains on duty during the 30 minutes and is paid for that time as hours worked; California law treats it as "on duty" precisely because Jordan Lee was not relieved of all duty. IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001 permits an on-duty meal period only when the nature of Jordan Lee's work prevents Jordan Lee from being relieved of all duty, and only by written agreement between Acme, Inc. and Jordan Lee. The DLSE has stated that whether the nature of the work prevents relief from duty is judged by an objective standard, not simply by the parties' say-so.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Unless the employee is relieved of all duty during a 30 minute meal period, the meal period shall be considered an “on duty” meal period and counted as time worked. An “on duty” meal period shall be permitted only when the nature of the work prevents an employee from being relieved of all duty and when by written agreement between the parties an on-the-job paid meal period is agreed to."
  — IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 11(A), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 11(A) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle04.pdf)
  "The test of whether the nature of the work prevents an employee from being relieved of all duty is an objective one. An employer and employee may not agree to an on-duty meal period unless, based on objective criteria, any employee would be prevented from being relieved of all duty based on the necessary job duties."
  — DLSE, Meal Periods FAQ, Cal. Dep't of Indus. Relations, Div. of Labor Standards Enforcement, Meal Periods FAQ (rev. July 11, 2012) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/FAQ_MealPeriods.htm)
  Known gap: This is one state's regulatory text (an IWC wage order provision) and a passage from a DLSE public guidance page describing that same regulatory structure — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer. The wage-order citation here restates the same provision already quoted in full in this corpus's separate Meal and Rest Break Policy document (its on_duty_meal_period clause); it is restated here because this information sheet is meant to be usable independently, not as a second, independent source for that text. The DLSE FAQ citation is a genuinely separate source (agency guidance, not the regulation itself), though it is not binding law and reflects the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement's own interpretation rather than a statute, regulation, or published court opinion.

REVOKING A WRITTEN ON-DUTY OR HEALTH CARE INDUSTRY MEAL-PERIOD AGREEMENT
A written on-duty meal period agreement between Acme, Inc. and Jordan Lee must itself state that Jordan Lee may revoke it in writing at any time. A related but distinct arrangement — the separate written waiver available under the wage order to health care industry employees working shifts of more than eight hours, covering one of their two meal periods — is revocable on different terms: Jordan Lee may revoke that waiver at any time, but only by giving Acme, Inc. at least one day's written notice. Revocation is therefore not a single, uniform rule across every meal-period arrangement described in this document; its terms depend on which specific arrangement is at issue.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The written agreement shall state that the employee may, in writing, revoke the agreement at any time."
  — IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 11(A), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 11(A) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle04.pdf)
  "The employee may revoke the waiver at any time by providing the employer at least one (1) day’s written notice."
  — IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 11(D), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 11(D) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle04.pdf)
  Known gap: This is one state's regulatory text (an IWC wage order provision), offered as documented evidence of what it says — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer. Both citations here are subdivisions of the same wage order section (§ 11 of IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001); they are treated as one source, not independent. The on-duty-agreement citation restates the same provision already quoted in full in this corpus's separate Meal and Rest Break Policy document; it is restated here so this information sheet can be read on its own.

AN INVOLUNTARY OR COERCED "WAIVER" DOES NOT EXCUSE THE MEAL PERIOD OBLIGATION
A meal-period waiver is valid only if it reflects Jordan Lee's genuine mutual consent. The California Supreme Court has stated, as quoted in the DLSE's own public guidance on meal periods, that "the wage orders and governing statute do not countenance an employer's exerting coercion against the taking of, creating incentives to forego, or otherwise encouraging the skipping of legally protected breaks." If a purported waiver is not the product of Jordan Lee's free choice — because it was coerced, pressured, or the product of an incentive to skip the meal period rather than a genuine mutual decision — it does not satisfy Cal. Labor Code § 512(a), and the meal period is treated as one Acme, Inc. did not provide. California law then requires Acme, Inc. to pay Jordan Lee one additional hour of pay at Jordan Lee's regular rate of pay for that workday — the same premium that applies to any other missed, short, or late meal period.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The wage orders and governing statute do not countenance an employer's exerting coercion against the taking of, creating incentives to forego, or otherwise encouraging the skipping of legally protected breaks."
  — DLSE, Meal Periods FAQ, Cal. Dep't of Indus. Relations, Div. of Labor Standards Enforcement, Meal Periods FAQ (rev. July 11, 2012) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/FAQ_MealPeriods.htm)
  "If an employer fails to provide an employee a meal period in accordance with an applicable IWC Order, the employer must pay one additional hour of pay at the employee's regular rate of pay for each workday that the meal period is not provided."
  — DLSE, Meal Periods FAQ, Cal. Dep't of Indus. Relations, Div. of Labor Standards Enforcement, Meal Periods FAQ (rev. July 11, 2012) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/FAQ_MealPeriods.htm)
  Known gap: This is one state's case law and agency guidance describing one state's statutory scheme (California) — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employment relationship, and not a claim that federal law imposes any comparable rule (it does not; federal law has no meal-period requirement to excuse or enforce). Both citations here are drawn from the same DLSE public guidance page; they are treated as one source, not independent — the coercion language originates in the California Supreme Court's Brinker decision and is quoted by the DLSE, and the premium-pay language restates the same one-additional-hour remedy documented, with its own independently verified citation to Cal. Labor Code § 226.7(b)-(c), in this corpus's separate Meal and Rest Break Policy document; it is not re-derived independently here.

SIGNATURE AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Jordan Lee acknowledges that this waiver applies only to a workday meeting the shift-length condition stated above, and that it does not waive Jordan Lee's right to a meal period on any workday where that condition is not met. Either Jordan Lee or Acme, Inc. may decline to continue this arrangement for a future workday; this document does not itself create a standing waiver beyond the workday(s) to which it applies.
